articles.title: Enamel thickness in the stem hylobatid Kapi ramnagarensis (Primates, Hylobatidae).
articles.authors: Alejandra Ortiz, Christopher C Gilbert, Xinyue Di et al.
articles.abstract: Enamel thickness has been extensively investigated in extant and fossil hominids, yet comparable data for hylobatids remain scarce. Existing studies are limited to Symphalangus syndactylus, Hylobates lar, and Hylobates muelleri and are based on relatively small samples. These studies have characterized enamel thickness as thin in Symphalangus and Hy. lar and intermediate-thin in Hy. muelleri. The polarity of these conditions within Hylobatidae also remains unresolved because stem representatives of the clade have only recently been discovered. Here, we used microcomputed tomography to examine lower third molar (M3) enamel thickness in the stem hylobatid Kapi ramnagarensis from the Miocene Lower Siwaliks locality of Ramnagar. We also provide new comparative data from 19 M3s of extant hylobatids representing all four living genera. Average (AET) and relative (RET) enamel thickness were quantified from two-dimensional virtual sections passing through the dentin horns of the two mesial cusps. The M3 of the single Kapi specimen exhibits enamel thickness values within the range observed in extant hylobatids, albeit near the lower end of that distribution, with RET most closely matching that of Hoolock leuconedys. Parsimony-based ancestral state reconstructions of M3 RET using gap-weighted coding hypothesize an intermediate-thin enamel condition at the base of Hominoidea. Within Hylobatidae, the ancestral state was likewise reconstructed as intermediate-thin enamel. Although RET provides valuable phylogenetic information, its interpretation remains challenging due to the limited data for early catarrhines and hominoids and the pervasive influence of homoplasy. Larger samples will help clarify patterns of enamel thickness variation within hylobatids and across Hominoidea.

articles.title: Marsupial fossil tracks reveal Eocene arboreal life in Antarctica.
articles.authors: Geovane Alves de Souza, Rafael Costa da Silva, João Felipe Leal Kaiuca et al.
articles.abstract: Antarctica is the only continent where land mammals are extinct today. Before the Eocene-Oligocene boundary (>38 million years ago), however, the "white continent" had a much milder climate that sustained a diverse fauna of terrestrial mammals. Several discoveries of fragmentary Eocene fossils suggest that Antarctica acted as a land bridge connecting South America to Australia, most notably marsupials. However, fossil mammals are scarce and restricted to a single location-Seymour Island. Here we present two well-preserved fossil tracks which are the second Antarctic fossil mammal outside Seymour Island and the oldest fossil tracks assigned to an opossum-like animal in the Cenozoic. They were found in the Fossil Hill Formation on King George Island (lower-middle Eocene) and exhibit possible opposable thumbs, suggesting an arboreal behavior observable in microbiotheriid and some extant didelphid marsupials living in South America today. They further coincide in time with the rise of scansorial lifestyle in several mammalian lineages. This ichnologic record offers a more comprehensive look into the dispersion and ecology of mammals through the Early Cenozoic of Antarctica, evidencing that small arboreal marsupials inhabited the South Shetland Islands during the Eocene. In addition, the new finding indicates that Antarctica was not merely a corridor, but a rich habitat of dense and productive forest canopies during the middle Eocene.

articles.title: Creating Consensus: Establishing a Definition of Sports Pharmacy and Its Emerging Role in Sports Medicine.
articles.authors: Claire May, Jessica Beal-Stahl, Athena Cannon et al.
articles.abstract: Sports pharmacy has become an increasingly recognized specialty within the broader pharmacy profession and serves as a complementary discipline to sport medicine. Yet, the field has lacked a formally established, internationally accepted definition. The absence of standardized terminology has hindered academic integration, interprofessional collaboration, and policy development. This work aimed to establish the first consensus-derived definition of sports pharmacy, accompanied by a responsibility statement to guide future education, certification, and research. In 2024, the US Sports Pharmacy Group (USSPG), comprising pharmacists, academics, anti-doping professionals, student pharmacists, and competitive athletes from diverse US states and international settings, convened a discrete subgroup, the Define Sports Pharmacy Taskforce, to lead the development of a formal definition of sports pharmacy. The taskforce conducted a thematic analysis of existing literature and reviewed 123 open-ended member responses collected between 2022 and 2024. Eight recurring practice themes emerged and informed iterative drafting cycles. Draft definitions were subsequently reviewed by interprofessional stakeholders, including physicians, elite athletes, and anti-doping practitioners. The resulting definition emphasizes medication management, anti-doping advocacy, interprofessional collaboration, athlete-centered ethical care, and the use of therapeutic and pharmacological strategies to optimize performance, support recovery, and protect sports integrity across all levels of physical activity. This consensus-derived framework provides standardized terminology to support the development of educational pathways, establish certification standards, and promote the integration of pharmacists into athlete support teams.

articles.title: Maximal Aerobic Capacity and Aging in Female Masters Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Shalaya Kipp, Kathryn F Larson, Diana B Collantes Hoyos et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Maximal aerobic capacity ( V ˙ O2max) represents the highest rate at which the body can use oxygen during intense exercise and is a key determinant of endurance performance. Although age-related declines in V ˙ O2max have been well documented in male individuals, less is known about this trajectory in female Masters athletes, defined as individuals aged 40 years or older who often engage in lifelong endurance training. OBJECTIVE: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify cross-sectional age-related differences in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes. METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 14 May, 2025 for studies reporting directly measured V ˙ O2max in female Masters endurance athletes aged 40 years or older. Eligible exercise modalities included running, cycling, swimming, and large muscle-mass ergometry, with testing conducted under standard environmental conditions. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using a modified Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled mean V ˙ O2max values were calculated for predefined age groups (40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70 years or older) using a random-effects meta-analysis. Meta-regression was used to estimate the relationship between age and V ˙ O2max. RESULTS: Sixty-nine studies, including 1903 female Masters athletes, met the inclusion criteria. Pooled mean relative V ˙ O2max was 45 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 43.0-46.8) in athletes aged 40-49 years, 40 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 38.5-41.7) in those aged 50-59 years, 35 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 33.2-37.1) in those aged 60-69 years, and 30 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 27.2-31.8) in athletes aged 70 years or older. Meta-regression demonstrated that each additional year of age was associated with a 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 lower V ˙ O2max (95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.44; P < 0.0001), equivalent to about 11.7% per decade. The association was consistent across testing modalities. CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrates a progressive age-related decrease in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes. Maximal aerobic capacity declines at an average rate of 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 per year after age 40 years, corresponding to approximately 11.7% per decade. This decline is evident across endurance sport disciplines and appears consistent with physiological changes associated with aging despite sustained endurance training. These findings provide female-specific reference values and a quantitative framework for future studies on aerobic capacity trajectories in female athletes. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S2RXZ ).

articles.title: Heat Training Practices in Elite and World-Class Athletes: A Review of Preparation Strategies for Competition in Hot Outdoor Environments.
articles.authors: Joshua D Elliott, Jamie Stanley, Peta Maloney et al.
articles.abstract: Heat acclimation (artificial exposure) and acclimatization (natural exposure) are key strategies for elite and world-class athletes preparing to compete in hot outdoor environments, aiming to reduce performance impairments and risk of heat illness. Evidence-based guidelines, primarily derived from laboratory studies in non-elite cohorts, recommend 10-14 consecutive days of heat exposure (60-90 min per day), initiated at least 2 weeks before competition in the heat, or earlier if re-acclimation is possible closer to the event. Sessions should elicit sustained elevations in core and skin temperature, skin blood flow, and sweating. However, logistical constraints, training demands, and tapering often limit protocol implementation in elite and world-class athletes, prompting the adoption of alternative approaches. This review synthesises observational studies documenting heat training practices in these athletes and evaluates their alignment with current guidelines. Eleven of the 12 studies included sport-specific heat exposure within preparation for competition in hot environments, often in similar or more severe environmental conditions than competition, with five studies incorporating post-exercise passive heating. However, heat intervention design, session structure, and monitoring of thermal and cardiovascular strain varied widely, with many reports lacking sufficient detail to determine their effectiveness at inducing and retaining adaptations outside laboratory-controlled settings. Nonetheless, initial reports indicate that classical markers of heat adaptation such as reduced exercise heart rate and core temperature, and increased plasma volume, are commonly observed. Standardized documentation of heat training characteristics is needed to assess their effectiveness in high-performance sport and refine evidence-based guidelines.

articles.title: Heart Rate Variability in Fighter Pilots: From Tactical Readiness to G-Tolerance Prediction.
articles.authors: João Bruno, Raynier Montoro-Bombú, Rohit Kumar Thapa et al.
articles.abstract: Fighter pilots are exposed to extreme physiological and psychological stressors including sustained positive head-to-foot acceleration (+Gz), high cognitive workload, and rapid decision-making demands. In such conditions, the ability to maintain autonomic balance is central to performance and safety. Heart rate variability (HRV) has emerged as a sensitive and noninvasive biomarker of autonomic regulation, reflecting the dynamic interplay between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity. This Current Opinion article explores the relevance of HRV in aviation medicine, emphasizing its predictive value for tactical readiness, resilience, and tolerance to gravitational stress. Evidence from centrifuge experiments and operational studies demonstrates that higher baseline HRV is associated with superior stress tolerance, reduced risk of loss of consciousness, and enhanced cognitive performance. Beyond acute stress assessment, HRV provides insights into recovery dynamics, fatigue status, and long-term resilience, supporting its use in readiness management and training optimization. Practical applications include daily monitoring to guide mission planning, individualized training prescriptions informed by autonomic profiles, and biofeedback interventions aimed at enhancing stress regulation. Emerging technologies such as wearable sensors, multimodal physiological monitoring, and machine learning further strengthen the translational potential of HRV for real-time telemetry and group-level readiness tracking. However, methodological challenges including individual variability, external influences, and the lack of standardized protocols must be addressed to enable operational integration. Overall, HRV represents a promising frontier for bridging physiology, performance optimization, and safety in high-stress environments.

articles.title: Rock Climbing and Nutrition: How Diet and Anthropometric Factors Influence Performance.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Laurel M Wentz, Sarah Radman, Alisha Farris et al.
articles.abstract: Wentz, LM, Radman, S, Farris, A, Farris, ZJ, and Kurtz, JA. Rock climbing and nutrition: How diet and anthropometric factors influence performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of diet and anthropometric characteristics on climbing performance. Rock climbers (N = 44: 52% women) completed a 3-day food record and International Society for Advancement of Kinanthropometry (ISAK) level 2 profile. Self-reported highest outdoor redpoint bouldering grade was used to categorize climber ability as intermediate or elite. Independent t-tests and Pearson's correlations were used for statistical analyses. Elite climbers (N = 11 men; 6 women) had similar body mass index (22.1 ± 1.8 vs. 22.1 ± 1.7 kg·m-2) and ape index (arm span/height; 1.02 ± 0.02 vs. 1.01 ± 0.03) compared with intermediate climbers (N = 10 men; 17 women). Dietary analysis showed energy intake was similar (42 ± 12 vs. 40 ± 10 kcal·kg-1 lean body mass, respectively), but protein intake was higher in elite climbers (1.6 ± 0.5 vs. 1.2 ± 0.4 g·kg-1 body mass; p < 0.01). Muscle mass was positively correlated with total energy intake (r = 0.56; p < 0.01) and protein intake (r = 0.65, p < 0.01). Elite climbers had greater muscle mass (31.4 ± 6.4 vs. 27.3 ± 5.4 kg; p = 0.03) and lower adipose mass (15.0 ± 2.0 vs. 18.5 ± 3.3 kg; p < 0.01) compared with intermediate climbers. Somatotype favored mesomorphy for all climbers (4.8 ± 0.9). Contrary to published reports showing energy restriction in rock climbers, our subjects consumed sufficient energy and met protein recommendations. Muscle mass was more important for climbing ability than total body mass or arm/leg length. Practical applications for climbing performance include improving modifiable characteristics, such as meeting protein and energy needs and improving muscle mass rather than restricting dietary intake, which may enhance strength-to-mass ratio, endurance, and overall climbing efficiency.

articles.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: David T Schilling, Timothy R Abraham, Ashraf Elazzazi
articles.abstract: Schilling, DT, Abraham, TR, and Elazzazi, A. Should they start or not? A comparative analysis of starter and nonstarter preseason fitness characteristics in NCAA Division III baseball. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Preseason fitness testing in baseball is a widely adopted practice to assess the physical preparedness of players. However, the relationship between these preseason fitness assessments, their ability to differentiate starters from nonstarters in the subsequent season, and their relationship to preseason coaching evaluations is not well-established. This exploratory study aimed to provide a preseason profile of men's NCAA Division III baseball players, compare the differences between starting and nonstarting players, and explore the relationship of these preseason measures to the offensive performance of the starting players at the completion of the season. Starters were considered any hitter who averaged at least 2 plate appearances per team game played or participated in at least 75% of the team's games. Twenty-six players performed 8 preseason fitness tests; and the head coach, blinded to all preseason fitness testing results, subjectively rated the players' batting (power, ball contact, and form) and running performance (speed, agility, and form), resulting in a total offensive performance score (TOPS). In-season offensive performance was measured by each player's on-base plus slugging percentage (OPS). Starters demonstrated significantly greater batted ball velocity, countermovement vertical jump height, unilateral lateral to medial jump distance, medicine ball throw velocity, and faster 60-yard dash and agility T-test times relative to nonstarters. Notably, no significant correlations were observed between any physical performance variable and OPS or TOPS, suggesting that preseason fitness testing may reflect athletic readiness but does not directly relate to offensive performance or coaching evaluation outcomes in this sample.

articles.title: Individualized Lactate Steady State Resolves the Discrepancy Between Maximal Lactate Steady State and Critical Speed in Running.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Ozgur Ozkaya, Hakan As, Arda Peker et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: We tested the hypothesis that maximal lactate steady state determined using a novel individualized blood lactate steady-state approach (MLSSInd) in running provides an accurate assessment of critical speed (CS). METHODS: Following a step incremental treadmill test, 8 endurance runners completed 5 constant-speed runs of up to 30 minutes for assessment of traditional MLSS (MLSSTrad) and at least 4 runs performed to the limit of tolerance for assessment of CS. MLSSTrad was defined as the highest running speed that resulted in changes in blood lactate concentration ([lactate]) of <1 mM between 10 and 30 minutes, whereas MLSSInd was determined by a breakpoint in the relationship between the rates of change of blood [lactate] between 10 and 30 minutes (or the end of exercise) plotted against the corresponding running speeds using a 2-segment linear regression. CS was calculated using the hyperbolic, linear, and 1/time models, and accepted using the model which yielded the lowest error. RESULTS: MLSSInd was significantly higher than MLSSTrad (14.0 [2.1] vs 13.2 [2.1] km·h-1, P < .001) but was not significantly different from CS (14.0 [2.1] km·h-1, P = 1.00). MLSSInd and CS were identical (r = 1.00, bias = -0.02 km·h-1, standard error of the estimate = 0.07 km·h-1, limits of agreement = -0.15 to 0.10 km·h-1). The rate of change in blood [lactate] at MLSSInd was greater than for MLSSTrad (0.07 [0.02] vs 0.04 [0.01] mM·min-1; P = .022). CONCLUSIONS: An individualized breakpoint in the relationship between the rates of change of blood [lactate] and running speed resolves the apparent mismatch between MLSS and CS in running and may better represent the heavy-to-severe intensity exercise domain boundary.

articles.title: Once Successful Junior Biathletes, but What Happened Next?
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Malin Jonsson Kårström, Glenn Björklund, Andreas Kårström
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate how successful junior biathletes performed as senior athletes and whether the transition rate (ie, achieving comparable performance rank as junior and senior) differed between nations with the highest numbers of athletes. METHODS: Juniors placed top 10 in individual competitions at Youth and Junior World Championships between 2006 and 2015 were chosen for further analysis. The biathletes were categorized into 5 different performance groups based on their senior performance (1: top 10 ranking in senior World Championships or Olympic Games [Top10-WCH], 2: top 40 ranking in World Cup (WC) total [Top40-WCtot], 3: competing in >20 individual WC competitions [>20 WCstarts] or 4: >20 International Biathlon Union Cup competitions [>20 IBUCstarts], and 5: competing in <20 individual International Biathlon Union Cup competitions [<20 IBUCstarts]). The distribution across the senior performance groups for the 4 nations with the highest number of athletes (France, Germany, Norway, and Russia) was compared with the overall sample. RESULTS: Out of 454 junior biathletes from 28 nations, 21.8% achieved a comparable performance rank as seniors (Top10-WCH), while 55.7% did <20 starts in the WC. For the 4 nations with the highest number of successful juniors, Russia demonstrated a greater percentage of athletes in the lowest performance category (<20 IBUCstarts) compared with the total sample (P < .05). CONCLUSION: The data showed a low transition rate from successful junior-to-senior level, and more than half of the biathletes did not compete regularly in the WC as seniors. The underlying reasons behind the different transition paths and possible differences between nations are of interest for future studies.

articles.title: Body Mass, Strength, Power, and Endurance Variations Across an Entire Season in Male Basketball Players.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Santiago Zabaloy, Irineu Loturco, Martín Barat et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to analyze changes in body mass, upper- and lower-boy strength, vertical jump performance, and endurance capacity in senior semiprofessional basketball players across 4 different time points (TPs) during the season. METHODS: Fifteen male basketball players (n = 15; age: 23.4 [3.4] y; height: 1.9 [0.1] m) volunteered to participate in this study. Participants were tested for body mass, 1-repetition maximum in the squat and bench press exercises, countermovement jump (CMJ) and loaded CMJ, and 30-15 intermittent fitness test. RESULTS: Significant increases were observed in absolute and relative 1-repetition maximum in the squat (P < .03; effect size [ES]: moderate to large) from TP1 to TP2, TP3, and TP4. Regarding CMJ, greater jump heights were observed at TP2 and TP4 when compared with TP3 (P < .015; ES: small). In the loaded CMJ (ES: moderate), loads were significantly greater at TP2, TP3, and TP4 compared with TP1 (P < .009; ES: moderate). Conversely, 30-15 intermittent fitness test measures showed small but nonsignificant increments (P < .086; ES: small). CONCLUSIONS: Lower-body strength and power measures improved during the preseason in male basketball players, with these athletes being able to retain strength levels across the in-season period, despite the congested competitive schedule. In contrast, CMJ performance did not change during the preseason but appeared to be negatively affected during the most competition-dense phase of the season (ie, TP3). Finally, endurance capacity and body mass remained relatively stable from the beginning of the preseason until the end of the season.

articles.title: The Relationship Between High-Intensity External Loads During Matches and Physical Fitness Characteristics in Male Collegiate Basketball Players.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Jun Koizumi, Takaki Yamagishi, Shunsuke Shiraki et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Basketball involves repeated high-intensity actions, including rapid accelerations, decelerations, and jumps. However, the association between match-derived external load metrics and physical fitness, particularly across match quarters, remains unclear. This study examined the relationships between quarter-specific high-intensity external loads during basketball matches and components of physical fitness. METHODS: Fifty male collegiate basketball players completed a simulated 32-minute match (four 8-min quarters) without substitutions; each player participated in 1 match. During the match play, 2 manufacturer-defined metrics, accumulated acceleration load (arbitrary units) and jump load, were quantified using inertial measurement units (KINEXON IMU). Accumulated acceleration load was calculated from changes in triaxial acceleration, and high-intensity acceleration load was defined using a predetermined acceleration threshold. Jump load represents the cumulative vertical mechanical load derived from jumping actions. On a separate day, peak oxygen uptake (V˙O2peak), mean power output during a repeated sprint ability test (eight 6-second cycle sprints), and countermovement jump height were assessed. The correlation between external load and physical fitness was analyzed using Spearman rank or Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient. RESULTS: High-intensity acceleration load across all quarters was significantly correlated only with V˙O2peak (rs = .285-.522, P < .05), with stronger associations observed in the later quarters. In contrast, jump load across all quarters was consistently correlated only with repeated sprint ability test mean power (rs = .340-.385, P < .05). CONCLUSIONS: V˙O2peak and repeated sprint ability were separately associated with different external load variables, which may provide useful insights for improving player-specific areas of weakness during a match.

articles.title: When Proxies Overshadow Actual Performance: Reaffirming First Principles in Applied Sport Science.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Irineu Loturco, Daniel Boullosa, Fábio Y Nakamura et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: In recent years, sport science has witnessed a growing emphasis on derived mechanical metrics and complex analytical approaches, often accompanied by claims that direct performance measures, such as jump height or sprint time are misleading or less informative than the proxies intended to explain them. This trend has contributed to a progressive shift away from the primary outcomes of athletic testing and toward secondary descriptors, frequently interpreted as superior indicators of performance. Using the vertical jump as a representative example, this commentary revisits fundamental foundations of classical mechanics and applied sport science to clarify the distinction between performance outcomes and mechanistic descriptors. The purpose of this commentary is to reinforce a fundamental principle of performance assessment: when the intended construct is task performance, direct outcomes, such as vertical jump height, horizontal jump distance, and sprint time should remain the primary reference. Mechanistic measures should be selected when they provide reliable and actionable information about how that outcome was achieved or why it changed. CONCLUSIONS AND PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: Actual performance outcomes, such as jump height, jump distance, and sprint time are the most meaningful, interpretable, and relevant indicators of athletic performance. Mechanistic variables and detailed analytical approaches may provide valuable insights into underlying movement strategies and efficiency, but they should complement, rather than replace, direct performance measures. Following Occam's razor, applied sport science should continue to embrace scientific advances while avoiding the unnecessary promotion of complex, time-consuming, and expensive technologies as indispensable tools for coaches and practitioners, thereby preserving confidence in simple, valid, and accessible measures of athletic performance.
